newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Slave's song brings African American grandma home.
newsitem.headline: Slave's song brings African American grandma home.

text.p: A song taken to the Americas by an African slave girl over two centuries ago helped African American grandmother Mary Moran discover the land of her ancestors.

Her "roots reunion" in the village of Senehun Ngola in southern Sierra Leone on Wednesday mingled joy and sadness for her and Baindu Jabati, a Sierra Leonian woman whose family had also kept the song alive through the generations.
But it also brought hope for the future, particularly for Jabati, one of tens of thousands of victims of Sierra Leone's brutal and often forgotten civil war.
"It is unexplainable. It was a moment of great joy and yet at the same time of great sadness for us both," Moran, 75, told Reuters on her return from the village.
"When we met in the middle of the village Baindu fell on her knees and laid her head on my lap and burst into tears."
Moran, from Harris Neck, South Carolina, traced her family origins to the south of the former British colony in West Africa via the song -- which is in the local Mende language.
Researchers took the song, which had been passed on from mother to daughter in Moran's family for over 200 years, and set out to find someone in Sierra Leone who recognised it.
They finally stumbled on Jabati after playing a recording of the song in numerous Mende villages in the south without success. Jabati learnt the song from her grandmother.
"There were tears in the eyes of people who had come with us from Freetown to witness this history-making event," Moran said after returning from a helicopter trip to the village.
Moran is from the Gullah community of coastal South Carolina.
Slavers took many ancestors of the community to the Americas from what was called the Rice Coast, the traditional rice growing region that is now Sierra Leone.
The Gullah community has preserved traditional foods -- rice dishes and okra soup -- which are still eaten in Sierra Leone.
Sierra Leone, racked by civil war since 1991, was set up under British protection in 1787 for freed slaves by opponents of slavery. It won independence in 1961.
President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule. He signed a peace deal with the rebels but implementation has proved difficult.
Moran said that Jabati was held by rebels for two years and was withdrawn and traumatised by the experience. "My heart bleeds for Baindu, my blood for Sierra Leone," she said.

She said that her family would remain in constant touch with Baindu and that two of her grandsons planned to return to Sierra Leone with their families next year to see how they could contribute to its reconstruction.
"We are holding a clan meeting in the United States when we get back to send help for our kin here," Moran said.
